description: We are a team of passionate students interested in space exploration, AI, healthcare, and technology. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we're developing a fluorescence microscopy detection application using computer vision and Python. We welcome creative, motivated individuals who enjoy solving real-world challenges. We're looking for teammates interested in machine learning, Python, biomedical science, data analysis, and UI/UX design. All experience levels are welcome!
summary: How can you detect diseases in space? Fluorescence microscopy is one way. It can be used to screen for microscopic disease markers in biological samples. However, fluorescence microscopes are heavy and costly, making them difficult to use in space. We have designed a low-cost, lightweight alternative that makes fluorescence microscopy more accessible in space environments. Our newly developed computer vision algorithm, trained on microscopic images obtained by NASA on the ISS, can help identify and diagnose disease markers in images captured by our low-cost fluorescence microscope. Our health tool will enable astronauts to monitor for disease markers on any mission, in space or beyond. It is crucial for astronauts, but it can positively impact everyone, including you.
details:
Project Glow is a low-cost, lightweight fluorescence microscopy system that integrates custom hardware and software to provide astronauts with advanced diagnostic capabilities in space.

The project addresses a critical gap in healthcare during spaceflight. Imagine an astronaut living on a lunar colony who develops a bacterial infection that does not respond to broad-spectrum antibiotics. How would they determine which pathogen is responsible and, consequently, which treatment to administer? Although targeted treatments may be available, astronauts need a reliable way to identify the underlying cause of an illness before selecting the appropriate medication. Basic health-monitoring tools, such as heart-rate monitors, cannot provide a definitive diagnosis, while conventional laboratory-grade diagnostic equipment is often expensive, bulky, and difficult to operate in microgravity.

Fluorescence microscopy offers a potential solution by detecting microscopic biological markers that emit light under specific wavelengths of illumination. However, conventional fluorescence microscopes are generally too expensive and heavy for practical use during spaceflight. We addressed this challenge by recognizing that conventional microscopes share many of the same fundamental optical components as fluorescence microscopes, yet are significantly cheaper and lighter. Building on this principle, we developed a proprietary fluorescence microscopy design that delivers advanced diagnostic capabilities at a fraction of the conventional cost and weight.

To complement the hardware, we developed software that makes the system accessible without requiring specialized technical training. Our Python-based computer vision pipeline uses OpenCV for image processing and NumPy for pixel-array calculations, statistical analysis, and intensity thresholding to identify and analyze diagnostic markers in images captured by our microscope. Results are presented through an interactive Streamlit web interface, incorporating Plotly visualizations such as fluorescence-intensity histograms and automated diagnostic threshold detection.

Recognizing that cellular behavior and biological markers can change under microgravity conditions, we also trained and evaluated our algorithms using microscopy datasets from NASA experiments conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS). When comparing the algorithm's outputs on NASA datasets with those obtained from images captured using our own hardware, we observed similar detection parameters. These preliminary findings suggest that our low-cost system has the potential to achieve comparable diagnostic detection capabilities.

Throughout development, we prioritized affordability, weight reduction, ease of operation, microgravity-specific biological considerations, and clear communication of diagnostic results. Ultimately, Project Glow aims to give astronauts the ability to identify illnesses and make informed treatment decisions during long-duration space missions. Although designed to address the unique healthcare challenges of astronauts, the potential applications of this technology extend far beyond spaceflight. By making sophisticated diagnostic microscopy more affordable, portable, and accessible, Project Glow could also help address healthcare challenges on Earth, including in remote communities and resource-limited medical facilities. Our goal is to make advanced diagnostic technology accessible not just to astronauts, but to everyone, including you.
